query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) can be used for a ductile–brittle–ductile transition due to their resistance to temper embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or 3D-printed HEA with a composition such as CoCrFeMnNi
generation.intervention: Variation of alloy composition and processing techniques
generation.structural_mediator: Suppression of temper embrittlement through the use of multiple principal elements in equal proportions
generation.mechanism: The multi-component nature of HEAs leads to a more stable microstructure, reducing the likelihood of dramatic ductility loss within a narrow temperature window
generation.predicted_outcome: A ductile–brittle–ductile transition with reduced embrittlement, resulting in improved ductility and toughness
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and processing techniques required to achieve optimal ductile–brittle–ductile transition behavior in HEAs are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of the ductile–brittle–ductile transition behavior of HEAs and conventional alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HEAs exhibit significant temper embrittlement within the specified temperature range, the hypothesis is falsified

frame.system: conventional alloys vs compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems
constraints: compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems

families.principle: Integration of experimental and simulation approaches to understand ductile–brittle–ductile transition
families.best_lever: Combining temperature-controlled mechanical testing with MD simulations

families.principle: Systematic variation of temperature to identify ductile–brittle–ductile transition
Modeling of atomic-scale mechanisms governing ductile–brittle–ductile transition
cues_for: compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems
families.best_lever: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of alloy systems

families.principle: Real-time observation of microstructural changes during ductile–brittle–ductile transition
families.best_lever: In-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or scanning electron microscopy (SEM)

levers.principle: Utilizing multiple principal elements in equal proportions to suppress temper embrittlement, thereby facilitating a ductile–brittle–ductile transition. Key parameters: alloy composition (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi), temperature range (-200°C to 200°C), and processing techniques (e.g., casting, 3D printing).

Applying in-situ heating and deformation to study the ductile–brittle–ductile transition in real-time. Key parameters: heating rate (1-10°C/min), deformation rate (10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1), and temperature range (-200°C to 500°C).

Manipulating grain boundary structures and properties to enhance ductility and reduce embrittlement. Key parameters: grain size (1-100 μm), grain boundary misorientation angle (0-60°), and temperature (20-500°C).
Introducing nano-scale precipitates to strengthen the alloy and improve ductility. Key parameters: precipitate size (10-100 nm), volume fraction (0.01-0.1), and distribution (uniform or random).

constraints: compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems
